nameStory: The bearberry willow gets its name from its incredibly low-growing, creeping habit that resembles the bearberry plant (Arctostaphylos uva-ursi). Both plants hug the ground in harsh mountain and arctic conditions, earning the same species name 'uva-ursi,' which literally means 'bear's grape' in Latin. While they're not related, early botanists noticed their similar prostrate growth form in extreme environments.
description: Bearberry willow is New England's most unusual willow - instead of growing upright like its tree and shrub relatives, this tough little plant sprawls flat along the ground like a living carpet. It's a prostrate shrub that rarely rises more than a few inches high but can spread several feet wide, with woody stems that creep along the surface. You'll only find this arctic refugee in New England's highest, most exposed mountain locations where few other woody plants can survive. Its tiny leaves and ground-hugging growth help it withstand fierce winds and extreme cold.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Completely prostrate, carpet-like growth that hugs the ground - unlike any other willow in New England. The woody stems creep horizontally and feel surprisingly sturdy for such a low plant.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very small, oval leaves that are much tinier than typical willows, with a leathery texture and often a slight shine on top. They feel thick and waxy, built to withstand harsh mountain conditions.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny catkins that appear close to the ground in early summer, much smaller than pussy willow catkins. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Only grows in the most extreme high-elevation sites in New England - exposed rocky summits, alpine zones, and areas above treeline where other willows cannot survive.

habitat: Bearberry willow clings to life in New England's most extreme environments - the windswept summits and alpine zones of our highest mountains, particularly in New Hampshire's White Mountains and similar high-elevation sites in Vermont and Maine. Look for it on exposed rocky ledges, alpine meadows, and areas above or near treeline where constant wind and harsh weather prevent most other woody plants from surviving. It often grows alongside other hardy alpine plants like diapensia and alpine azalea.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge late in the season due to the harsh mountain climate, appearing as tiny green ovals close to the ground. Growth begins slowly as snow melts from the high peaks.
seasonality.summer: Small catkins appear in early to mid-summer, and the plant displays its full carpet of small, leathery leaves. This is the best time to observe its unique prostrate growth form.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, though the change is subtle. The woody stems become more visible as a low network across the rocks.
seasonality.winter: Bare woody stems create an intricate pattern across the ground, often buried under snow for months. The prostrate branching structure remains visible during brief snow-free periods.

funFact: This tiny willow is essentially a living fossil from the Ice Age - when glaciers retreated, bearberry willow stayed behind on New England's highest peaks, creating 'sky islands' of arctic plant life that have been isolated for over 10,000 years!
confusionNotes: The prostrate growth makes it nearly impossible to confuse with other willows, but it might be mistaken for bearberry (Arctostaphylos) or other low alpine shrubs. Remember: if it's growing flat as a pancake on a high mountain summit and has tiny willow-like leaves, it's bearberry willow - no other willow in New England grows this way.
contextualKnowledge: Despite sharing the name 'bearberry' and similar growth habits, bearberry willow is completely unrelated to true bearberry (Arctostaphylos uva-ursi). This naming similarity reflects how plants in harsh environments often evolve similar survival strategies, a phenomenon called convergent evolution.
compareHints: Bearberry willow is instantly distinguished from all other New England willows by its unique prostrate growth - every other willow species grows upright as shrubs or trees. While pussy willow, black willow, and other relatives can reach 10-30 feet tall, bearberry willow never rises more than a few inches off the ground. Its extreme habitat preferences also set it apart - no other New England willow tolerates the harsh alpine conditions where bearberry willow thrives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many willow species, pussy willow stands out for its exceptionally soft, silvery catkins that appear before the leaves.
Among New England's willows, heart-leaved willow stands out for its combination of thick, persistently fuzzy-bottomed leaves with heart-shaped bases.
Among New England's willows, Bebb's willow stands out for its dense thicket-forming habit and adaptability to various soil types.

Among New England willows, rusty willow is most similar to grey willow (Salix cinerea), but rusty willow's twigs have that distinctive reddish-brown coloration versus grey willow's more grayish twigs.
Among New England's many willow species, black willow stands out as the largest tree form with the darkest bark.
Among New England willows, prairie willow is unique in preferring dry, sunny sites while most others need moist to wet conditions.
Grey willow differs from native pussy willow by having much more pronounced silvery-gray, woolly leaf undersides and tends to form denser thickets.
Among New England's many willows, silky willow stands out for its distinctly silky leaf undersides - most other willows have smooth or only lightly hairy leaf backs.
Interior sandbar willow stands out from other New England willows by having the narrowest leaves in the genus - much thinner than pussy willow's oval leaves or black willow's lance-shaped ones.
Meadow willow is much shorter and more colony-forming than most other New England willows like black willow or pussy willow.
Among New England's willows, shining willow stands out for its exceptional height and mirror-like leaves.
Among New England's willows, purple willow is unique for its purple-red bark and blue-green leaves - pussy willow has gray bark and broader leaves, while black willow has dark, furrowed bark.

Unlike the familiar pussy willow with its large, fuzzy catkins and broad leaves, or the water-loving black willow with its narrow leaves, tea-leafed willow has those distinctive thick, oval leaves with prominent parallel veining.
Among New England willows, sage-leaf willow is unique for its distinctly fuzzy, silvery leaves that truly resemble herb sage.
Among New England's many willows, balsam willow is unique for its strong balsam fragrance - most other willows are essentially scentless.
Among New England willows, least willow is unmistakable due to its ground-hugging growth - all other willows in our region grow as upright shrubs or trees.
Bog willow differs from its willow relatives by staying much shorter and preferring acidic bog conditions rather than streamside locations.
Among New England's many willows, satiny willow stands out for having the most dramatically silvery leaf undersides—much more pronounced than the similar silky willow or sage-leaf willow.
Among New England's willows, white willow stands out for its especially silvery leaf undersides and larger mature size.
Unlike the familiar pussy willow with its large, showy catkins and bigger leaves, or the tall black willow found along rivers, Labrador willow stays remarkably small and compact.
Unlike native New England willows such as pussy willow or black willow, dappled willow has variegated foliage and often opposite leaves rather than alternate ones.

Among New England willows, autumn willow stands out for its completely hairless leaves and stems - unlike pussy willow's fuzzy twigs, silky willow's silky leaf undersides, or meadow willow's slightly hairy stems.
Among New England's willows, blueleaf willow is distinguished by its blue-green foliage color - most other willows have bright green or silvery leaves.
Unlike other New England willows such as pussy willow or black willow that have upright or spreading branches, weeping willow is unmistakable due to its pendulous, drooping branch structure.
Among New England's willows, peachleaf willow stands out for its impressive tree size - most of our native willows like pussy willow or silky willow are shrubs or small trees.
Unlike most New England willows which have narrow, lance-shaped leaves, goat willow stands out with its broad, oval, wrinkled leaves that look more like those of a poplar or apple tree.

Basket willow stands out among New England's willows for its extremely narrow leaves and exceptionally long, straight, flexible branches - most native willows like pussy willow or black willow have broader leaves and shorter, less flexible shoots.
Among New England's many willow species, rose-gold pussy willow stands out for its ornamental catkin colors - most native willows like common pussy willow have plain silver-gray catkins.
